candidates.text: When an ocean cable breaks, who fixes it?
A cable ship does, and it lays new ones too.
Cable engines can feed 240 m of cable a minute.
Goliath was the first ship to lay an ocean cable, in 1850.
It crawls at about eight knots so the cable settles.
Cable-laying ship failed because a cable ship pays out cable at low speed along a carefully mapped route.
What stops if cable-laying ship stops?
Every metre of the route is mapped as it goes down.
So the fastest links on Earth depend on its slowest ships.
When repair ships are busy or far away, a damaged cable stays down longer and traffic runs on thinner backup routes.

paragraphs.text: When an ocean cable breaks, who fixes it?
Cable ships are limited to eight knots while laying cable, and they map the cable’s path to place it correctly on the seabed. Every new or repaired submarine cable depends on such vessels.
There are two main types: smaller, maneuverable repair ships that can also lay cable, and larger, less agile laying ships with parallel drums that lay cable faster. Both use linear cable engines.

The linear cable engine feeds up to 240 m per minute, includes a brake, and can reverse to retrieve cable. Grapple systems on synthetic ropes pull damaged sections, while plows use water jets to bury cable three feet deep.

Modern hybrid ships like USNS Zeus can both lay and repair cable, travel 15 knots and lay 1,600 km to 2,700 m depth. Its design mirrors the Great Eastern and it runs MakaiLay software used by most cable ships.
Cable ships are built around oversized sheaves that guide the cable across the hull, positioned at the bow, the stern, or both, depending on the vessel’s generation.
Their official designations commonly begin with the prefix “C.S.”—for example, CS Long Lines—signalling their role as cable layers.

The earliest transatlantic telegraph link was laid by cable‑laying vessels between 1857 and 1858, achieving a brief operational window before technical misuse caused failure; a later successful deployment occurred in 1866 when the SS Great Eastern laid two durable cables, establishing a lasting conduit between Europe and North America.
A cable ship pays out cable at low speed along a carefully mapped route, and in repairs grapples the cable from the seabed and splices it on deck.
Cable ships are purpose‑built, equipped with specialised handling gear and staffed by trained crews; they cannot be improvised from ordinary vessels.

When repair ships are occupied or distant, a damaged cable remains offline longer, forcing traffic onto thinner backup routes; cable layers are deep‑sea vessels built to install underwater cables for telecom, power, or military purposes.
Regional maintenance agreements keep repair ships on standby, and route diversity keeps traffic moving while a repair waits.
